captions.text: Parity tells us whether a whole number is odd or even.
Think of an even number as pairs, and an odd number as
pairs with one left over.
Look for a move or arrangement that must preserve
parity.
One quick check can rule out a long search.
AMC practice may hide odd and even structure in jumps,
paired objects, or a game where each move changes some
pieces.
A Rossmoyne style proof can use parity or a two-colour
pattern to explain why a proposed arrangement is
impossible.
Is the sum of thirteen and eighteen odd or even?
Try to decide by pairing.
Think about how many unpaired counters each addend
would have.
thirteen has one extra counter after pairing.
eighteen is fully paired, so it contributes no extra
The total has one extra and is odd.
The exact sum is thirty-one, which confirms the pairing
argument.
A counter starts at thirteen on a number line.
Each move adds or subtracts an even number of steps.
Can it ever reach eighteen?
The length and direction may change on each move.
Adding an even number is adding entire pairs.
Subtracting an even number also removes entire pairs.
Neither change affects the leftover one.
The counter starts at odd thirteen, and every later
position must remain odd.
The target eighteen is even, so it is unreachable.
Start with the numbers three, seven, nine, fourteen and
nineteen.
A move replaces any two numbers by their sum plus one.
Keep going until only one number remains.
Is that final number odd or even?
Does the choice of partners matter?
The original sum is fifty-two.
Replacing two entries by their sum plus one adds
exactly one to the total, whatever pair you choose.
Every move decreases the number of entries by one.
Five entries need exactly four moves to make a single
entry.
Add four to the original total.
The last number is fifty-six, so it is even regardless
of how you merge.
Check by merging from left to right.
Then think about swapping the first pair.
The order changes the intermediate values, but each
move adds one to the total.
In a longer version, a list of n entries takes n minus
one moves.
This lets you answer even when drawing every move would
take too long.
Try a parity question before calculating a big total.
Label each value odd or even and see how the labels
combine.
A matching parity does not prove that every move is
allowed.
Use a construction as well whenever the question asks
what can be achieved.
Mark what one move does to parity.
Decide whether the leftover changes, stays fixed, or
follows a pattern.
Check whether the target has the required parity or
colour balance.
Write one sentence explaining why every legal move
obeys that rule.
